subject: Physics
scope: Thirteen original AQA Year 1 Physics Waves mock recall items, focusing on evidence and explanations not separately covered in the v159 audit.
notes: AQA 3.3.1.2–3.3.2.2: sound/microwave interference, single-slit appearance and wavelength effect, grating geometry, stationary-wave reasoning, polarisation and EM speed. No experimental set-up instructions. Does not certify complete bullet-by-bullet syllabus coverage.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why can two coherent sound sources produce alternating loud and quiet regions?
cards.back: Their sound waves superpose constructively at some positions and destructively at others.
accept: Their sound waves superpose constructively at some positions and destructively at others.
Some places have constructive interference and others destructive interference.
Interference causes positions of reinforcement and cancellation of sound.
The waves add in phase at loud places and cancel out of phase at quiet places.
reject: Because one speaker makes a higher-frequency sound.
The sounds always cancel everywhere.
The speed of sound changes between loud and quiet positions.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For two coherent sound waves reaching a point, what path difference gives destructive interference?
cards.back: An odd multiple of half a wavelength, (m + ½)λ.
accept: An odd multiple of half a wavelength, (m + ½)λ.
Half a wavelength, three halves, five halves and so on.
An odd number of half wavelengths.
(n + 0.5) times the wavelength.
reject: An integer number of whole wavelengths.
A path difference of zero.
Any path difference gives destructive interference.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What do alternating strong and weak microwave signals at different positions demonstrate?
cards.back: Constructive and destructive interference from superposition of electromagnetic waves.
accept: Constructive and destructive interference from superposition of electromagnetic waves.
Microwaves can reinforce and cancel by interference.
Superposition gives positions of strong and weak microwave intensity.
Electromagnetic waves show constructive and destructive interference.
reject: Microwaves are longitudinal waves.
Interference proves microwave frequency changes with position.
Strong and weak regions show microwaves cannot superpose.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In the derivation of the grating equation, what is the path difference between light from adjacent slits at angle θ?
cards.back: d sin θ, where d is the slit spacing.
accept: d sin θ, where d is the slit spacing.
The adjacent-slit path difference is d sin theta.
d multiplied by the sine of the diffraction angle.
Slit spacing times sin theta.
reject: d divided by sin theta.
n times the speed of light.
The wavelength divided by slit spacing.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does the grating equation d sin θ = mλ give bright orders only for integer m?
cards.back: Light from adjacent slits must arrive in phase with a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths.
accept: Light from adjacent slits must arrive in phase with a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths.
Constructive interference requires an integer multiple of wavelength.
The path difference must be m wavelengths for reinforcement.
The waves reinforce when neighbouring-slit paths differ by complete wavelengths.
reject: A half-integer path difference always produces a bright maximum.
All angles give constructive interference.
Light from neighbouring slits must have different frequencies.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do you find the slit spacing for a grating labelled 600 lines per mm?
accept: d is 1.67 micrometres.
The line spacing is about 0.00000167 m.
Convert to 600000 lines per metre and take the reciprocal.
reject: d equals 600000 metres.
d is 1.67 millimetres.
The separation is 600 metres.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a fixed grating and non-zero order, what happens to the diffraction angle as wavelength increases?
accept: The diffraction angle increases.
The angle becomes larger.
Longer wavelengths have a greater angle in the same order.
The diffraction maximum moves further from the central maximum.
reject: The angle becomes smaller.
The angle stays the same for every wavelength.
The order number must become negative.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a single slit of fixed width, how does a longer wavelength change the central diffraction maximum?
accept: It becomes wider.
The central maximum spreads out.
The central diffraction peak has greater angular width.
Increasing wavelength broadens the central bright maximum.
reject: The central maximum becomes narrower.
The central maximum disappears completely.
Wavelength has no effect on diffraction spread.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the qualitative pattern for monochromatic light passing through a single narrow slit?
cards.back: A broad bright central maximum with weaker side maxima separated by dark regions.
accept: A broad bright central maximum with weaker side maxima separated by dark regions.
A wide central bright fringe with fainter bright fringes on either side.
The central maximum is widest and brightest; side maxima are dimmer.
A bright wide centre with alternating dark and weak bright side fringes.
reject: All bright fringes have the same width and intensity.
Only a single sharp point with no spreading is observed.
The central bright maximum is always weaker than the side maxima.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In successive snapshots of a stationary-wave pattern, what happens to the positions of the nodes?
cards.back: They stay fixed and have zero displacement.
accept: They stay fixed and have zero displacement.
Nodes remain at the same positions with no displacement.
The nodes never move along the string.
All nodes stay fixed at zero displacement.
reject: Nodes travel along the string with wave speed.
Nodes are where the amplitude is greatest.
Every node shifts by half a wavelength each cycle.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What two travelling waves form a stationary wave by superposition?
cards.back: Waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions.
accept: Waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions.
Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions.
Oppositely travelling waves of the same frequency superpose.
A forward and reflected wave of the same frequency overlap.
reject: Two waves travelling in the same direction only.
Two waves with completely different frequencies always form a stable standing wave.
Two opposite waves must have different wavelengths in the same medium.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Which component of a linearly polarised light wave is transmitted by an ideal linear polariser?
cards.back: The electric-field component parallel to its transmission axis.
accept: The electric-field component parallel to its transmission axis.
The electric field aligned with the transmission axis.
The part of the light's electric field parallel to the polariser axis.
Oscillations parallel to the polarising filter's transmission direction.
reject: The component perpendicular to the transmission axis is transmitted unchanged.
Light is a longitudinal wave so it cannot be polarised.
The polariser changes the light's frequency into sound.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do the speeds of different electromagnetic waves compare in a vacuum?
cards.back: All travel at the same speed, c, approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
accept: All travel at the same speed, c, approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum.
Their speed in vacuum is the same, about 3 x 10^8 m/s.
Radio, visible light and X-rays all have the same vacuum speed.
reject: Radio waves are always slower than visible light in vacuum.
Higher-frequency EM waves are faster in vacuum.
Only visible light travels at c.
